criteria.reasoning: The bottom line states "Agnes Gund died on September 18, 2025, at her home in Manhattan, aged 87," and the red flags repeat "She has died (September 18, 2025)." Nowhere is she treated as living.
Section 2 says "Source: inherited wealth. Her father died in 1966 and left her a large fortune in trust." Section 1 names him as George Gund II, president of the Cleveland Trust Company.
It states she "was president from 1991 to 2002 and also chairman from 1993 to 1995. Afterwards she was President Emerita and Life Trustee," which matches the required years.

It says "she founded it in 1977, with her own money, after New York City's fiscal-crisis budget cuts virtually eliminated art from the public schools. It places professional artists in public-school classrooms."

It says "In 2017 she privately sold Roy Lichtenstein's Masterpiece (1962) for $165 million," and the gift table lists "Art for Justice Fund: founding gift from the Masterpiece sale | $100,000,000 | 2017." It describes the fund as a criminal-justice-reform fund.
The report says the fund "closed on June 30, 2023, after more than $127 million in grants," and a red flag reads "The Art for Justice Fund is closed (June 30, 2023)."

It names the "AG Foundation (EIN 34-1606084)" and says its "surviving trustees are her daughters Catherine Gund and Anna Traggio." No other AG Foundation trustee is named, and Gund is not presented as a current decision-maker.
The gift table lists AG Foundation grants to Studio In A School Association of $1,369,599 (2020), $545,619 (2021), $277,771 (2022) and $1,085,000 (2023), all of which match the 990-PF figures.

The current size is given as "$34.3 million at book value ($50.0 million at market value)" at the end of 2024, with grants of $3.9 million in 2024 and $8.1 million in 2023. The one older figure is labeled with its year ("$35.3 million in 2020").

A red flag says "Studio in a School is the incumbent... A new NYC arts-education program competes directly for the same family's arts-education dollars unless it is clearly complementary." The strategy also says to "Position next to Studio in a School, not against it" or partner with it.

It recommends "No ask to Agnes Gund. Remove her from solicitation lists, and plan no cultivation, ask or bequest request addressed to her." The $10,000–$25,000 ask is directed to the foundation via its trustees.

It states "No unsolicited proposal. The AG Foundation's Forms 990-PF state that it gives only to preselected organisations and doesn't accept unsolicited requests," and recommends a personal introduction to the trustees instead.

It says "The George Gund Foundation is not a route for this program. Its arts grants go to organisations in or directly serving the City of Cleveland," and adds that it does not prioritise arts education outside the Cleveland Metropolitan School District.

It warns "Don't credit her with her brothers' gifts," attributing The Gund at Kenyon to Graham and the Foundation Fighting Blindness co-founding to Gordon, with Agnes as "a supporter." Sports teams are not attributed to her.

All the checked facts agree with the fact sheet: her death date, birth, MoMA years, Studio founding, the $165M sale and $100M gift, the AG Foundation figures and trustees, the Studio grant amounts, the $3.28M four-year total, the Christie's estimates, Hasna Muhammad as Studio chair, and the George Gund Foundation chair and limits. I found no contradiction.
